extracted.intended_audience: academic researchers, graduate students, grant applicants, and program officers interested in how disciplinary cultures shape evaluation of research proposals
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes evaluative criteria and disciplinary standards used by multidisciplinary panels to assess research proposals, highlighting what counts as 'excellence' across fields (history, anthropology, political science, economics). Useful for applicants and reviewers preparing or judging funding proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrity of the research
rubrics_metrics.description: Integrity of the research (panelist phrasing: "Integrity of the research").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluators look for research based on honest, rigorous practice; this is presented as a core convention of excellence that reviewers across some subfields agree upon. Anti-patterns include sloppy data collection, misrepresentation, or lack of methodological transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigorous testing, data collection, and methodology
rubrics_metrics.description: "Is research based in some kind of rigorous testing, in terms of the way in which it’s collected, the ideas behind [it], the methodologies that are used to follow up the conceptualization of a project."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposals should show clear methodological plans and rigorous data collection strategies tied to project conceptualization. Examples: concerns about projects that rely on secondhand survey data without contextualization. Anti-patterns: vague or method-driven claims without concrete procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of thought and articulation
rubrics_metrics.description: "Clarity of thought, having very clear ways of articulating what it all means."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposals must state aims, significance, and interpretation in clear, accessible language. Jargon-heavy or self-referential prose that obscures significance can harm evaluation (political scientist lament about jargon-laden anthropology proposals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation, relevance, and explanation of importance
rubrics_metrics.description: "Having some way of interpreting for others why [it is] important, and what it means, and what relevance it has to a particular field of knowledge or to a larger body of knowledge."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers expect proposers to explain the project's relevance and situate contributions within the field or broader literatures. Weakness: projects that fail to explain significance or implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality and contribution to existing work
rubrics_metrics.description: "Explaining what contributions it’s going to make, and making some important contributions along the lines of originality, along the lines of . . . building on . . . the work of others in very significant ways, perhaps branching out, expanding other important work."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposals should articulate novel contributions or significant extensions of prior research. Mere repetition or minor add-ons to existing literature are less likely to be rated excellent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual knowledge and language competence
rubrics_metrics.description: Panelist critique: reviewers expect applicants (especially in anthropology) to have contextual knowledge and language skills relevant to the study area (example: reviewers noting applicants who "didn’t speak or read a single language other than English").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For area-based or ethnographic projects, demonstrable familiarity with local context, history, and language is important. Anti-patterns: proposing cross-cultural studies without travel, linguistic ability, or documentation of contextual competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Face-to-face fieldwork and immersion (ethnographic depth)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The critical value of face-to-face field work or gaining people’s trust; of getting at the social world through actual personal interaction."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anthropological excellence often hinges on evidence of intensive ethnographic engagement and trust-building. Proposals that spread fieldwork across too many sites ("more than two locales") may be judged infeasible or "lite anthropology."

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of scope and feasibility (number of sites/locales)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concerns that projects involving more than a few locales may be infeasible ("Whenever I see an anthropological project that involves more than two locales, or three maybe, it seems to me impossible that that person will be able to do that").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers assess whether proposed scope matches time, resources, and methods. Overambitious multi-sited designs without justification are penalized; feasible, well-justified scopes are favored.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engagement with neighboring disciplines and literatures
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique that some anthropology proposals "will often not cite a single thing written by a non-anthropologist" as an indication of insularity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panels value awareness of relevant literatures beyond the proposer's home discipline when appropriate; failure to engage cross-disciplinary work can be seen as a sign of narrowness or ignorance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of jargon; clear, comprehensible writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple panelists report difficulty evaluating "jargon laden" proposals and emphasize the need for clear language (political scientist: had to work harder to figure out significance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write proposals in language intelligible to non-specialist panelists on multidisciplinary committees. Excessive jargon or self-referential terminology can lead to misunderstanding or low scores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alignment between stated aims and actual methods (proposal fidelity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances where reviewers said proposals "didn’t actually live up to what the person said he/she was going to do."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposals should be internally consistent: objectives, methods, and expected outcomes must align. Discrepancies between claims and methods reduce credibility and scores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological fit: triangulation versus intensive fieldwork
rubrics_metrics.description: Debate whether combining methods ("triangulating") is as desirable as traditional intensive fieldwork; some value multi-methods, others prioritize long-term immersion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justify methodological choices in disciplinary terms and explain why chosen methods are the best fit. Be aware that different evaluators prize different methodological approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative sophistication, formalization, and mathematical methods
rubrics_metrics.description: In political science and economics, "math and formalization have come to define 'good methods'" and "how quantitatively sophisticated you are" is often a marker of excellence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For fields valuing formal methods, demonstrate appropriate quantitative skills, formal modeling, or simulation as required. Lack of quantitative rigor can disadvantage applicants in these disciplines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contribution to generalizable theory or nomothetic claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Expectation among some political scientists that contributions should be to "a generalizable theory of politics, or nomothetic laws of politics... making a theoretical contribution."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If claiming theoretical contribution, make clear how findings generalize beyond case(s) and how they advance theory; interpretivist or case-specific contributions should be framed for their own value when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem-driven versus method-driven research orientation
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinction drawn between problem-driven approaches (valued by some) and method-driven research (valued by others). The Perestroika Movement sought more balance favoring problem-driven work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Articulate whether the project is driven by an important substantive problem and explain method choices as serving that problem, not the reverse. Panels may reward problem-driven clarity in some contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstration of scientific norms and methodological rigor (case selection, robustness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reference to Designing Social Inquiry and the emphasis on demonstrating that qualitative methods can produce rigorous inferences (concern with case selection, demonstration of rigor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Qualitative proposals should address issues like case selection, inference validity, and robustness to satisfy reviewers seeking scientific rigor comparable to quantitative work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence and convincing empirical support
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluators note: "Either they have the evidence or they don't. If they have the evidence, then it's nicely done."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide plausible, concrete evidence (pilot data, preliminary results, archival access, or clear data sources) and explain how evidence will be obtained and analyzed; unsupported claims are weak.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity about theoretical assumptions and worldview
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism that economists (and others) may be unwilling to explain their theoretical worldview; reviewers expect clarity about assumptions underlying models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make theoretical assumptions explicit and transparent so reviewers from other traditions can understand the basis of claims; opacity about assumptions reduces persuasiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluative culture fit (discipline-specific criteria vs cross-disciplinary applicability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Panelists sometimes mobilize discipline-specific criteria (e.g., anthropological emphasis on contextualization) that may not be applicable to other fields; risk that reviewers judge across incompatible standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying to multidisciplinary review, explain and justify disciplinary standards used and, where possible, translate them into criteria accessible to non-specialists. Anticipate diverse expectations on panels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation, reflexivity, and ethics of speaking for others
rubrics_metrics.description: Post-Writing Culture concerns: pay attention to the literary quality of writing, epistemological and moral difficulty of "speaking for others," and questions of representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address reflexivity and ethical issues of representation explicitly (how the researcher relates to subjects, positionality, and limits of representation). Failure to attend to these can trigger disciplinary objections in anthropology and cultural studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-reductionist understanding of the research subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Panelists emphasize the need to "make sense of the object in a non-reductionist manner."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overly reductive models of complex social phenomena unless justified; demonstrate awareness of nuance and complexity appropriate to the discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding political sanctimoniousness as an evaluative lens
rubrics_metrics.description: Panelists criticize using political commitments as grounds for dismissing other methods ("linking [other methods] to ... serving the interests of colonialism, imperialism, racism...").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep political positioning from substituting for methodological critique. While political relevance may be a legitimate evaluative dimension, dismissing work solely on ideological grounds is seen as an anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Readable proposal for interdisciplinary panels (translate disciplinary conventions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Several respondents stressed that proposals must engage conventions of excellence "that a good proposal pretty much, no matter what the field, can engage with."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft proposals so central claims and methods are intelligible to scholars from other fields: define terms, justify methods, and show significance in broadly comprehensible ways.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scoring practice: independent ranking and 'cream rising to the top'
rubrics_metrics.description: Panelists prepared matrices rating proposals by total score ("sum of the scores given by each panelist") and observed homogeneity in scores where some proposals had "practically perfect scores."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that many panels use independent pre-meeting scores aggregated into matrices; strong proposals that are widely recognizable as high-quality may avoid extended debate. Prepare a proposal that can be positively assessed independently by varied reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fit with funder-specific standards and preferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Different funders are perceived as using different standards (e.g., NSF favoring rational choice/formal methods; SSRC more open to qualitative work).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor proposals to the norms and priorities of specific funders (methods, theory, and presentation). Researching funder preferences can improve alignment and success.
